subject: Biology
title: Freshwater Ecosystems
description: A fast breakdown of Freshwater Ecosystems for builders.

hook.text: Rivers, lakes, and wetlands hold less than 1% of Earth's water but support 10% of all species.

buildup.text: Freshwater ecosystems provide drinking water, irrigation, and food for billions of people.

discovery.text: Wetlands act as natural sponges—they absorb floods and filter pollutants from water.

twist.text: Freshwater species are declining twice as fast as land or ocean species worldwide.

climax.text: Dams, pollution, and water diversion threaten these ecosystems that humanity depends on.

punchline.text: One percent of the water. Ten percent of the life.

quiz.question: What natural function do wetlands perform?

details.summary: Freshwater ecosystems include rivers, lakes, wetlands, and streams, covering less than 1 percent of Earth's surface but supporting about 10 percent of all known species. They provide drinking water, irrigation, and fisheries while serving as critical wildlife corridors.
details.whyItMatters: Freshwater biodiversity is declining faster than marine or terrestrial biodiversity. Pollution, damming, water extraction, and climate change threaten these vital ecosystems that billions of people depend on for clean water and food.
takeaways: Freshwater habitats cover under 1 percent of Earth but hold 10 percent of species
Wetlands filter pollutants and buffer floods naturally for free
Dams fragment rivers affecting fish migration and sediment transport

faq.question: Why is freshwater biodiversity declining so rapidly?
faq.answer: Freshwater systems are impacted by pollution, damming, water extraction, invasive species, and climate change simultaneously. Their small extent concentrates species in vulnerable areas. An 84 percent average decline in freshwater vertebrates since 1970 has been documented.

faq.question: How do wetlands benefit the environment?
faq.answer: Wetlands act as natural water filters, removing pollutants and excess nutrients. They absorb flood waters like sponges, recharging groundwater. They store carbon, provide fish nurseries, and support exceptional biodiversity relative to their small area.
